passages.t: Before the king, and no power over the day of death
passages.happening:
‘Who is like the wise man? Who knows the interpretation of a matter? A man’s wisdom brightens his face’ (verse 1).

Then counsel for life at court. ‘Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God’ (verse 2). Do not rush out of his presence or stand firm in a bad cause, for he does what he pleases (verse 3), and no one can question him (verse 4). ‘Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm, and a wise heart knows the right time and procedure’ (verse 5).

‘Since no one knows what will happen, who can tell him what is to come?’ (verse 7). ‘As no man has power over the wind to contain it, so no one has authority over his day of death. As no one can be discharged in wartime, so wickedness will not release those who practice it’ (verse 8). And there is a time when one person rules over another to his own harm (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Absolute monarchy was the normal form of government in the ancient world, whether in Solomon's court, the Persian empire, or the Greek kingdoms that came after Alexander. A subject had little protection against a ruler who could do as he pleased. The oath before God in verse 2 probably means an oath of loyalty sworn to the king in God's name.

Court manners could be a matter of life and death. To leave the king's presence suddenly might look like rebellion. Esther risked her life by entering the king's presence uninvited. Wise officials learned the right time and the right way to speak, and wisdom writings from Egypt and Mesopotamia give similar advice. This is counsel for living under that kind of power. It is not a teaching that rulers are always right, and verse 9 says plainly that rulers can harm those under them.

Verse 8 lists things beyond human control. The Hebrew word for wind, ruach, also means breath or spirit, so the verse may mean that no one can hold on to his own life when death comes. Once a war was under way there was no leaving it, and death is like that.
passages.later: Esther knew the danger of verse 3: anyone who came to the Persian king without being summoned could be put to death, ‘Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live’ (Esther 4:11). And the psalm says what verse 8 says: ‘What man can live and never see death?’ (Psalm 89:48).
passages.asks: No one has power over the day of his death. Ask how that truth might change the way you spend this day. And ask where you live under someone else's power, and what wisdom you need to speak well there.

passages.t: Justice delayed, and the fear of God
passages.happening:
The Teacher saw the wicked buried with honor, praised in the very city where they had done their deeds. ‘This too is futile’ (verse 10). ‘When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil’ (verse 11).

‘Although a sinner does evil a hundred times and still lives long, yet I also know that it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence’ (verse 12). It will not go well with the wicked, because they do not fear God (verse 13).

Then: “There is a futility that is done on the earth: There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve” (verse 14).

‘So I commended the enjoyment of life, because there is nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry’ (verse 15), a joy that goes with a person in the work God gives.
passages.hearers:
Verse 10 seems to describe wicked people who came and went at the holy place, presumably the temple, being buried with honor and praised in the city where they had done evil. The Hebrew is difficult, and translations differ over whether the wicked are praised or forgotten.

Verse 11 is a sharp observation: when justice is slow, people grow bold in doing wrong.

Then verses 12 to 14 set two things side by side that seem to pull against each other. The Teacher knows it will go well with those who fear God. He also sees the righteous getting what the wicked deserve.
passages.later: The psalmist wrestled with the same sight: ‘For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked’ (Psalm 73:3), until he entered God's sanctuary and ‘discerned their end’ (Psalm 73:17).
passages.hard:
How can the Teacher say that it goes well with those who fear God (8:12), and also that the righteous get what the wicked deserve (8:14)?

The two statements sit side by side, and interpreters handle them in different ways.

One view is that verses 12 and 13 state traditional wisdom, which the Teacher quotes in order to set it against what he has seen in verse 14. On this reading the tension is deliberate and unresolved. A second view is that the Teacher believes both: he knows by faith that God's justice will win out, and he sees that it has not yet. A third view, close to the second, reads verses 12 and 13 as looking past what can be seen to a final judgment, which the book's last verse makes plain (12:14).

What the chapter does not do is resolve the tension by denying either side. It refuses to call injustice justice, and it refuses to give up on the fear of God.
passages.asks: The Teacher held on to the fear of God while seeing injustice clearly. Ask what injustice you have seen that tempts you to give up trusting God. And ask what it would mean, like him, neither to deny it nor to let it have the last word.

passages.t: No one can find out the work of God
passages.happening:
The Teacher set his mind to know wisdom and to watch the work done on earth, the kind of task that keeps a person from sleep day and night (verse 16).

‘I saw every work of God, and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning; even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with the verb to find, as chapter 7 did. No one can find out the whole work of God, however hard they search, and even the wise who say they know cannot.

This is not despair. It is humility about the limits of human understanding, and it prepares for chapter 9, where the common fate of death presses the question harder still.
passages.later: Paul ends a long reflection on God's ways in the same place: “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!” (Romans 11:33). And Job's friend asks, ‘Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty?’ (Job 11:7).
passages.asks: Even the wise cannot find out the whole work of God. Ask what you are losing sleep trying to understand. And ask whether you can trust him with what you cannot comprehend.
